summary: Matthew L. Miller's Cool Green Science blog post (June 21, 2021) describes six birds with surprising predatory or unusual feeding habits: pelicans, great blue herons, turkeys, crows, kelp gulls, and vampire finches. The examples range from pelicans swallowing pigeons and herons impaling fish and baby alligators, to kelp gulls tearing flesh from living whales and vampire finches drawing blood from boobies. The post argues that many birds not thought of as predators are opportunistic and will take larger prey when available. Reader comments add further anecdotes such as a snowy egret swallowing a snake and a robin pecking a hiker's scab.
one_line: A Nature Conservancy blog list of six birds, including pelicans, herons, turkeys, crows, kelp gulls and vampire finches, with surprising predatory feeding habits.
key_facts: The post '6 Surprising Tales of Predatory Birds' was written by Matthew L. Miller and published June 21, 2021 on the Cool Green Science blog.
The author's chickens ate a vole that wandered into the chicken pen, and a Rhode Island red was seen devouring a quail chick.
The world's eight pelican species are famous for their beaks and large throat pouches used to scoop up fish.
The pelicans in London's St. James Park are fed fish by groundskeepers but are known to supplement their diet by gulping down city pigeons.
Great blue herons often impale larger fish with their dagger-like bills, shaking them to break or relax the sharp spines before gulping them down.
Great blue herons eat snakes and baby alligators, stuffing seemingly impossible prey down their throats.
The wild turkey was once nearly extirpated from much of North America but has made an astounding comeback.
Researchers have documented wild turkeys eating tadpoles, bluegills, snakes and lizards.
Research found that roadkill makes up less than five percent of American crows' calories, according to Corvid Research.
Kelp gulls eat living whale flesh, pulling off strips of flesh and blubber from southern right whales off the Valdes Peninsula in Argentina.
The kelp gull feeding behavior was first documented in 1972, and by 2008, 77 percent of the whales in the area had suffered wounds from feeding gulls.
Vampire finches of the Galapagos Islands switch to pecking blue-footed and Nazca boobies and sipping their blood during times of scarcity.
Researchers believe the vampire finch and booby relationship developed as mutually beneficial, with finches pecking parasites off the boobies.
A commenter reported seeing a snowy egret swallow a snake longer than the bird's neck in Florida.
The author notes that very few birds are strictly herbivorous and many are opportunistic, taking much larger prey if the opportunity presents itself.
